board.title: The board and its squares
board.summary: 64 squares, and every square has a name.

steps.text:
Welcome to Chesti! The board has **64 squares**, alternating light and dark.

First rule: the square in the **bottom right corner** must be **light**.

The files are letters from `a` to `h`, and the ranks are numbers from `1` to `8`. So every square has a name like an address, like `e4` and `d5` that are lit up in front of you.

Each player has 16 pieces:

- 8 **pawns**
- 2 **rooks** in the corners
- 2 **knights** next to the rooks
- 2 **bishops** next to the knights
- 1 **queen** on a square of her own color (the white queen on a light square)
- The **king**, the most important piece in the whole game

White always moves first.
Let's try it: move the pawn in front of the king to the `e4` square. You can drag it with your finger, or tap it and then tap the square.
steps.hint: The pawn in front of the king is on `e2`. Take it to `e4`.

steps.text:
The pawn is the smallest piece, but it has real value.

- It moves **forward only**, one square.
- **On its first move only**, it can go two squares.
- **It never goes backward.**
This pawn hasn't moved yet. Move it **two squares** in one go.
The pawn **doesn't capture forward**, it captures **diagonally** (one square diagonally forward). Capture the black pawn.
steps.hint: The pawn captures diagonally forward, toward `d5`.

steps.text: If there is a piece directly in front of the pawn, **the pawn is blocked** and can't move, even if that piece belongs to the opponent. Here the two pawns face each other and neither can move.

The rook moves **in a straight line**: forward, backward, right, left, any number of squares as long as nothing blocks the way.

It's worth about **5 pawns**.
The black knight is on the same file as your rook. **Capture it!**
And this time on the same rank. Capture the bishop.

bishop.title: The bishop
bishop.summary: Diagonally, and on one color all game.

steps.text:
The bishop moves **diagonally** any number of squares.

That's why a bishop that starts on a dark square **stays on dark squares the whole game**, and the one on a light square stays on light. It's worth about **3 pawns**.
There's a loose rook. Can the bishop capture it? Try.

The queen moves like a **rook and a bishop combined**: straight and diagonally, all the way.

That's why she's the strongest piece, worth about **9 pawns**. Take good care of her!
Capture the knight with the queen.

The knight is the strangest piece: it moves **two squares in one direction and then one square sideways**, like the letter **L**.

It's **the only piece that jumps over other pieces**. It's worth about **3 pawns**.
Capture the pawn with the knight.
At the start of the game, the knight is the only piece (besides the pawns) that can move, because it jumps. Develop either knight.
steps.success: Exactly! The best square for the knight is usually `f3` or `c3`, toward the center.

steps.text:
The king moves **one square** in any direction.

The king **can't be captured**, and the whole point of the game is to trap the opponent's king. And you can't move your king to a square the opponent attacks.
The king captures too. Capture this pawn.

values.title: Captures and piece values
values.summary: Capture the more valuable piece first.

steps.text:
To know when a trade is good for you, memorize these values:

- Pawn = **1**
- Knight = **3**
- Bishop = **3**
- Rook = **5**
- Queen = **9**
- King = priceless

If you give a knight and take a rook, you came out ahead.
Your queen can capture the pawn or the rook, and both are unprotected. Which one will you take?
steps.hint: The rook is worth 5 and the pawn is worth 1.

steps.text:
When a piece attacks the king, it's called **check**. You must respond right away in one of three ways:

- **Move the king** away
- **Block** the path with a piece
- **Capture** the piece giving check
You're Black and the rook is giving check to your king. **Move the king.**
The black bishop is giving check. This time **block the check with the knight**.
steps.hint: The knight can jump to `d2` or `c3` and stand in the bishop's way.

steps.text: Your turn to give check. Check the black king with the rook.

mate.title: Checkmate
mate.summary: Check and no escape = you win.

steps.text:
**Checkmate** means the king is in check, and there's no way to escape, block, or capture the piece giving check. The game is over right then.

Look here: the rook is giving check, and the black king is trapped behind its pawns. That's checkmate.
Make the same move: **checkmate in one move**.
Checkmate with the queen. There's more than one solution.
steps.hint: Your king covers `a7` and `b7`. You need to cover the back rank.

castling.title: Castling
castling.summary: One move that protects the king and brings out the rook.

steps.text:
**Castling** is the only move where you move two pieces: the king moves **two squares** toward the rook, and the rook jumps **over and lands next to it on the other side**.

Conditions:

- The king and the rook **haven't moved** before.
- No pieces between them.
- The king is **not in check**, and won't pass through or land on an attacked square.
Castle kingside (short castling): drag the king **two squares right**.
And now long castling, on the queen's side: drag the king **two squares left**.
Here White **can't castle short**: the black bishop attacks `f1`, and the king can't pass through an attacked square. But long castling is allowed.

en-passant.title: En passant
en-passant.summary: The rule many people don't know.

steps.text:
If the opponent's pawn moves two squares from its start and lands **next to** your pawn, you can capture it as if it had moved only one square.

But note: you must capture it **on the very next move**, otherwise the chance is gone.

notes.0: The black pawn moved two squares and passed next to the white pawn, as if running away from it.
notes.1: The white pawn **captures it as if it had moved only one square**, and lands on `d6`. This is **en passant**.

steps.text: Black just moved `d5` two squares. **Capture it en passant!**
steps.hint: Your pawn on `e5` can go to `d6` and capture the pawn next to it.

steps.text:
If a pawn reaches **the last rank**, it must promote to any piece: queen, rook, bishop, or knight. Usually we choose the **queen** because she's the strongest.

So you can end up with two or three queens!
Take the pawn to the end of the board and **promote it to a queen**.
steps.hint: Take the pawn to `e8` and choose the queen.

draws.title: Draws and stalemate
draws.summary: How a winning game becomes a draw.

steps.text:
**Stalemate**: it's Black's turn, his king is **not in check**, but he has no legal move. Then the game is a **draw**!

White was winning by a big margin here, and threw the game away. Watch out for it.
Give **checkmate** without causing stalemate.
steps.hint: If you play `Qc7` it's stalemate! Look for a check that covers the back rank.

steps.text:
There are other ways to draw:

- **Not enough material to mate**: like king against king, or king and bishop against king.
- **Threefold repetition**: if the same position happens 3 times.
- **Fifty-move rule**: 50 moves by each side with no capture and no pawn move.
- **Agreement**: both players agree to a draw.

back-rank.title: Back rank mate
back-rank.summary: The king trapped behind its pawns.

steps.text: The black king is trapped behind its three pawns, and nobody protects the back rank. **Lock him in.**
The black rook is the only piece protecting the back rank. Remove it and give mate.
**How do you protect yourself?** Move a pawn in front of your king one square (like `h6` here) to give it a **window** to escape through. Players call it "luft".

queen-mate.title: Queen and king mate
queen-mate.summary: The queen traps, the king comes closer.

steps.text:
The queen alone can't deliver mate, **the king has to help**.

The plan:

- The queen shrinks the black king's space until he reaches the edge.
- Your king comes closer.
- Watch out for **stalemate**: always leave the black king a square to move to until the moment of mate.
The two kings face each other. Give mate in one move.
And here too. There are two solutions!

ladder.title: Ladder mate with two rooks
ladder.summary: The two rooks walk the king up, step by step.

steps.text:
The rook on `h4` locks the whole fourth rank. The other rook will give check on the fifth rank, so the king goes up one step. Then the two rooks swap roles until the king reaches the edge.

Keep the rooks **far from the king** so he can't come near and capture them.
Drive the black king up to the last rank and give mate. Start with a check from the rook on `g1`.
steps.hint: Each time, move the rook behind, and give check on the rank where the king stands.

rook-mate.title: Rook and king mate
rook-mate.summary: The kings face each other, and the rook locks the rank.

steps.text: With one rook the plan is the same: push the black king to the edge, and keep your king **right across from his** (this is called the opposition). Then a check from the rook on the edge is mate.
Give the mate.

center.title: Control the center
center.summary: The four squares in the middle are the treasure.

steps.text:
These four lit squares are **the center**. A piece in the center attacks more squares and reaches anywhere faster.

That's why the most famous first move is the king's pawn or the queen's pawn two squares.
Start the game with a move that controls the center.
steps.success: Excellent! `e4` and `d4` are among the strongest first moves.

develop.title: Develop your pieces
develop.summary: Knights and bishops first, and castle early.

steps.text:
After the pawns, **develop the minor pieces** (knights and bishops) quickly, and **castle** so the king is safe.

Watch this game and follow every move.

notes.2: The knight comes out and attacks the black pawn.
notes.3: Black protects his pawn and develops a piece at the same time.
notes.4: The bishop comes out to a nice square and looks at `f7`, Black's weakest square.
notes.6: Early castling: the king is safe and the rook is closer to the center.
notes.9: Both sides developed their pieces calmly. This is the **Italian** opening.

steps.text: Develop the bishop to an active square so you can castle next.
steps.success: Nice! `Bc4` is the Italian and `Bb5` is the Spanish (Ruy Lopez).

early-queen.title: Don't bring the queen out early
early-queen.summary: An early queen gets chased and wastes time.

steps.text: The queen is an expensive piece, so any cheap piece that attacks her forces her to run. That way the opponent develops his pieces **while chasing you**, and you waste time.

notes.2: White brought the queen out on move two and threatens `e5` and `f7`.
notes.3: Black protects `e5` and develops a piece.
notes.5: And chases the queen away with a pawn.
notes.6: The queen goes back, and threatens `f7` again.
notes.7: The knight blocks the threat and develops a new piece.
notes.9: Black developed 3 pieces and is ready to castle, while White wasted moves with the queen.

steps.text:
Summary of the opening principles:

- Control **the center** with pawns.
- Develop **knights and bishops** before rooks and the queen.
- **Castle** early.
- Don't move the same piece twice without a reason.
- Don't bring the **queen** out early.
- Connect the two rooks.

**The fork**: one piece attacks two or more pieces at the same time. The opponent can save only one.

The knight here gives check to the king and at the same time attacks the rook. The king has to run, and the rook is lost.
Make a knight fork and win the rook.
steps.hint: Look for the knight square that attacks the king and the rook together.

steps.text: Even the pawn makes forks! Attack the knight and the bishop together.
steps.success: The pawn on `d4` is protected by the other pawn and attacks two pieces. One of them is lost.

steps.text: A queen fork: check the king and attack the rook in one move.

pin.title: The pin
pin.summary: A piece can't move because of what's behind it.

steps.text:
**The pin**: a piece attacks a piece, and behind it is a more valuable piece.

The black knight here is **pinned**: if it moves, the king would be in check, and that's illegal. So the knight is **paralyzed**.
The knight is pinned and can't escape. **Attack it with something cheap** and win it.
steps.hint: Attack the pinned knight with a pawn, it can't escape.

skewer.title: The skewer
skewer.summary: The valuable piece in front, and another behind it.

steps.text: **The skewer** is the opposite of the pin: the valuable piece (usually the king) is **in front**, and when it runs, the piece behind it is exposed.
Give a check that makes the king run, and capture the queen behind him.

discovered.title: The discovered attack
discovered.summary: One piece moves, and the piece behind it attacks.

steps.text:
**The discovered attack**: the rook is standing behind the bishop. If the bishop moves, the rook gives check to the king. So the bishop can go **anywhere** and attack anything, while the opponent is busy with the check.

If both pieces give check together, it's called **double check**, the strongest kind.
Move the bishop with a discovered check and win Black's most valuable piece.

smothered.title: Smothered mate
smothered.summary: The king is suffocated among his own pieces.

steps.text: The black king is hemmed in by his own pieces. Only the knight can reach him. **Give mate.**
This is the most famous move in chess, **Philidor's legacy**: sacrifice the queen so the rook locks in its own king, and then the knight finishes.
steps.hint: Sacrifice the queen on `g8`. The rook is forced to capture it.
steps.success: An artist! You sacrificed the queen and gave mate with the knight.

square-rule.title: The square rule
square-rule.summary: Can you catch the pawn or not? Calculate it in a second.

steps.text:
Picture a **square** in your head from the pawn to the end of the board (from `a4` to `e8`).

If the king can **enter that square** on his turn, he will catch the pawn. If not, the pawn will promote.
You're Black. Enter the square so you can catch the pawn.
steps.success: There, you entered the square, and whatever the pawn does, you'll catch it.

opposition.title: The opposition
opposition.summary: The kings face each other, and whoever is on move loses.

steps.text:
**The opposition**: when the kings face each other with one square between them, **the side on move is forced to give way**.

In a king and pawn ending, if your king gets **two ranks in front of the pawn**, you'll usually win.
The king is walking in front of the pawn, not behind it. **Advance your king** to the sixth rank.
steps.hint: Your king must reach the sixth rank before the pawn.
steps.success: Exactly! Your king is in front of the pawn, and Black can't stop it.

weak-squares.title: Weak squares
weak-squares.summary: A square no pawn can protect = a free home for the opponent's pieces.

steps.text:
A weak square is a square **no pawn can ever protect**, like `d5` in front of you: Black moved the `c` and `e` pawns, so no pawn will ever come back to cover that square.

Pieces love these squares because they stand there **without anyone chasing them away**.

Look at White's knight on `c3`: it has its eye on `d5`. If a knight lands on a weak square inside your half of the board, it will cause you trouble on every move.

The rule: **think twice before moving a pawn**, because every pawn move leaves behind squares that can never be protected again.
You're White. Put the knight on the weak square `d5`.
steps.hint: The knight on `d4` can jump to the weakest square in Black's camp.
steps.success: Exactly! The knight stands in the middle of the board and nobody can chase it away.

open-files.title: The open file
open-files.summary: The rook loves an empty file like coffee in the morning.

steps.text:
An open file is a file with **no pawns at all**. A rook standing on it rules the position: she looks into the opponent's camp and waits to enter on the seventh or eighth rank.

Here White and Black are standing on the same `d` file. Whoever controls this file has a real advantage.

The coffee rule: **a rook on the seventh rank = a nightmare for the opponent.** She eats the pawns that haven't moved yet, and traps the king on the last rank.

That's why when you take an open file, your next goal is right away: enter the seventh rank through it.
You're White. Use the open file and enter the seventh rank with the rook.
steps.hint: The rook on `d1` can enter the file all the way to the seventh rank.
steps.success: You entered the seventh rank! The pawns on `b7` and `f7` are now in your sights.

outposts.title: The outpost
outposts.summary: A knight sitting in the heart of the opponent's camp that nobody can chase.

steps.text:
An outpost is a square that is **protected by your pawn** and at the same time **the opponent can't chase you from with a pawn**.

White's most famous outpost is `e5` when Black plays `d5` early: the knight on `f3` can jump there and become the king of the center.
You're White. Put the knight on the outpost `e5`.
steps.hint: The knight on `f3` has a golden square in the center.
steps.success: The knight on `e5` is like a pasha: it attacks `c6`, `f7`, `g4` and `d7`, and no pawn will chase it.

steps.text:
Don't worry if the opponent trades a piece to capture your knight on the outpost: he'll usually pay a price, like giving you a bishop for a knight or opening a file for you.

The point isn't the knight itself, the point is that **its presence narrows the opponent's choices**.

good-bad-bishop.title: The good bishop and the bad bishop
good-bad-bishop.summary: Is your bishop good or bad? Ask where your pawns stand.

steps.text:
The **bad** bishop is the one whose pawns stand on the same color as its squares, so they lock it in like a wall.

The **good** bishop is the one whose pawns are on the other color, so it's free to run along the diagonals.

Look at White's bishop on `e2`: White's pawns are on a mix of light and dark squares, so it's an in-between bishop, but if all the pawns were on light squares it would be a bad bishop.

If you find your bishop is bad, you have 3 solutions:

1. **Move the pawns** to the other color if you can.
2. **Take the bishop out** of the pawn wall before it gets locked in.
3. **Trade it** for the opponent's good bishop or for a suitable piece.
You're White. Bring the bishop out from behind the pawns to an active square on `g4`.
steps.hint: The bishop on `e2` has an open diagonal toward the kingside.
steps.success: The bishop came out to `g4` and became active: it looks at `h5` and pressures the kingside.

knight-vs-bishop.title: Knight or bishop?
knight-vs-bishop.summary: Two worth 3 points each, but not always equal.

steps.text:
The knight and the bishop are each worth 3 points, but their real value depends on the shape of the position:

- **Closed position** (lots of pawns jammed in the center): the knight is better, because it jumps over the crowd.
- **Open position** (empty files and diagonals): the bishop is better, because it hits from far away.

In closed positions like this one, the knight circles around the weak squares one by one and harasses the king and the pawns.

And if you have **two bishops against a bishop and a knight or two knights** in an open position, that's an advantage called "the bishop pair", and it wins a lot of games by itself.
You're White. Activate the knight from `e2` to `c3`.
steps.hint: The knight on `e2` needs to enter the game through the lane next to the pawns.
steps.success: The knight came in through `c3` and now looks at `d5` and `b5`. In closed positions the knight is the star of the show.

pawn-majority.title: Pawn majority
pawn-majority.summary: 3 against 2 on one wing = a promotion factory in the endgame.

steps.text:
Look at the kingside: White has 3 pawns against 2 for Black. This is called a **majority**.

In endgames, this majority moves forward together until it creates a **passed pawn** with no enemy pawn in its way, and then it runs until it promotes.

How do you advance the majority? The rule: **move the pawn that has no enemy pawn facing it first** (here `g`), then push the rest behind it.

A famous mistake: moving the wrong pawn so it gets blocked, and your majority becomes a standing piece of wood.
You're White. Start advancing the kingside majority with the right move.
steps.hint: Start with the pawn that has an empty road ahead.
steps.success: Right! `g4` first, then `f4` and `h4` behind it, and the majority moved like a wave.

prophylaxis.title: Prevention is better than cure
prophylaxis.summary: Before you make your plan, ask: what does the opponent want to do?

steps.text:
Prophylactic play is when you **prevent the opponent's plan before it starts**, instead of only thinking about your own plan.

The strongest players in history like Petrosian, Karpov and Carlsen were masters of this: they make you unable to play what you wanted in the first place.

Ask yourself the golden question after every opponent move: **"What does this move want to do?"**

If you see Black's bishop heading to `g4` to annoy you, a move like `h3` before it gets there stops the whole idea without losing anything.
You're White. Play the prophylactic move that prevents `Bg4`.
steps.hint: One small pawn move will keep Black's bishop off an annoying square.
steps.success: Exactly! `h3` closed `g4` in the face of Black's bishop before it even thought about it.

space.title: Space and the squeeze
space.summary: Whoever has more space, their pieces play more comfortably.

steps.text:
Space is counted by the number of squares your pawns look at in the opponent's half of the board.

Whoever has more space can **move his pieces from one side to the other quickly**, and whoever has less space is cramped and his pieces bump into each other.

If you're the one who is cramped, the solution isn't to watch: **trade pieces**. Every trade gives you more room.

And if you're the one with the space, do the opposite: **avoid trades** and keep the opponent's pieces crowded.
You're Black and cramped in this position. Play the trade that relieves you: `Ne4`.
steps.hint: Your knight on `f6` can trade itself for White's knight on `c3`.
steps.success: Right! This trade eases the squeeze: one piece fewer in a small space = longer breath.

anastasia-mate.title: Anastasia's mate
anastasia-mate.summary: A queen sacrifice opens the h file and the rook finishes.

steps.text:
Anastasia's mate is one of the most beautiful mates in history: a knight closes the escape squares, a queen is sacrificed on `h7`, and a rook lands on the `h` file to give mate.

The pattern is named after an old German novel where it appeared on the board.

The order matters: first the knight gives check from `e7` so the king runs to the corner, then the queen sacrifices herself on `h7`, and when the king takes her he is standing on the open `h` file... and the rook is ready.
You're White. Carry out the full Anastasia's mate: 3 moves for you and the opponent will reply in between.
steps.hint: Start with a check by the knight, and then think about a sacrifice on `h7`.
steps.success: Full Anastasia's mate! Knight + queen sacrifice + rook on the file. A masterpiece.

arabian-mate.title: The Arabian mate
arabian-mate.summary: A rook and knight trap the king in the corner. The oldest known mate.

steps.text:
This is the oldest mate pattern on record, written in Arabic manuscripts more than a thousand years ago, when the Arabs were the masters of chess in the world.

The idea: **the knight covers two squares next to the king** (`g8` and `h7` from `f6`), and the rook gives mate protected by the knight.

Look at the knight on `f6`: by itself it locks `g8` and `h7`. So the black king stands on just one square, and all that's missing is the rook arriving.

All that's missing: a rook reaching `h7` while protected.
You're White. Carry out the Arabian mate in one move.
steps.hint: The rook on `a7` reaches the corner in one move.
steps.success: The Arabian mate! The knight protects the rook and closes the escape. A mate over a thousand years old.

greco-mate.title: Greco's mate
greco-mate.summary: A bishop on the long diagonal and a queen giving mate on h7.

steps.text:
Gioachino Greco, an Italian who lived in the 17th century, used to write down his games and sell them. One of his most famous ideas: the **queen and bishop battery** on the `b1-h7` diagonal.

The bishop on `c2` looks at `h7`, and the queen will use that protection.
The black king in the corner is trapped among his pawns: `f7` and `g7` lock him in, and if the queen reaches `h7` protected by the bishop it's mate right away, because `g8` is in the queen's range.
You're White. Deliver Greco's mate in one move.
steps.hint: The queen on `h5` and the bishop on `c2` look at the same square.
steps.success: Greco's mate! The queen is protected by the bishop from afar, and the king has nowhere to go.

morphy-mate.title: Morphy's mate
morphy-mate.summary: A rook on the last rank and a bishop locking the diagonal.

steps.text:
Paul Morphy, the American of the 19th century, used to beat anyone blindfolded. His famous mate: **a rook on the eighth rank + a bishop locking the long diagonal**.

Look at the bishop on `b2`: it covers `g7` and `h8` by itself.

The black king is locked in a small corner: `f7` and `h7` are his pawns, and `g7` and `h8` are in the bishop's range. So the eighth rank is his whole life.

Any rook that reaches the eighth rank here = mate.
You're White. Deliver Morphy's mate in one move.
steps.hint: The eighth rank is empty in front of your rook.
steps.success: Morphy's mate! The rook on the eighth rank and the bishop locking the diagonal. Exactly like Morphy used to do.

hook-mate.title: The hook mate
hook-mate.summary: A knight, a rook and a pawn make a net around the king.

steps.text:
The Hook Mate is a complete fishing net: a **knight** covers the escape, a **pawn** protects the knight, and a **rook** delivers the blow.

The shape of the three pieces around the king looks like a hook, and that's where the name comes from.
You're White. Catch the king with the hook mate.
steps.hint: The knight on `f6` covers `h7` and `g8`. The rook knows the way.
steps.success: The hook mate! The rook is protected by the knight, and the king is caught in the net.

epaulette-mate.title: The epaulette mate
epaulette-mate.summary: The king is smothered between two pieces beside him like a soldier's epaulette.

steps.text:
The epaulette is named that because the king stands **between two of his own pieces** on the same rank, like the two stars on an officer's shoulder.

The rooks on `e8` and `g8` don't protect the king, they're what smothered him.
You're White. Smother the king between his epaulettes.
steps.hint: Your queen on `h4` can reach a diagonal and give check from next to the king.
steps.success: The epaulette mate! The king is smothered between his rooks, and the queen from `f6` controls everything.

dovetail-mate.title: The dovetail mate
dovetail-mate.summary: The queen next to the king, and the opponent's pieces lock the rest.

steps.text:
The Dovetail is the sibling of the epaulette, but on the diagonal: the king is hemmed in by his own pieces on two sides, and the queen gives mate from an adjacent square.

Here Black's knight on `f8` and rook on `h8` are smothering their own king.
You're White. Find the mate from a square adjacent to the king.
steps.hint: The pawn on `e5` will protect the square the queen is heading to, and the bishop on `c4` covers the escape.
steps.success: The dovetail mate! The queen is protected by the pawn, the bishop locks `g8`, and Black's pieces smothered their own king.

blackburne-mate.title: Blackburne's mate
blackburne-mate.summary: A knight, a queen and a bishop trap the castled king.

steps.text:
Joseph Blackburne, the Englishman nicknamed "the Black Death", specialized in kingside mates.

His net: a **knight on `g5`** protects `h7`, and a **bishop** locks the escape square `f8` from afar.
You're White. Deliver Blackburne's mate in one move.
steps.hint: The knight on `g5` is ready to protect your queen on the most dangerous square.
steps.success: Blackburne's mate! The queen is protected by the knight, and the bishop locks `f8` from the other end of the board.

mate-kq.title: Mate with king and queen
mate-kq.summary: Cut the board off from the king, bring your king closer, and watch out for stalemate.

steps.text:
The queen alone can't give mate, **your king has to help**. The method is called "cutting off the board":

1. The queen makes an imaginary line the king can't cross.
2. Each time the king moves, you shrink the line.
3. When the king is pushed to the edge, bring your king closer and deliver the mate.

A very important warning: **stalemate**. If the black king isn't in check and has no legal move, the game is a draw and all your work is gone.

Before your final move, always ask: does the king have a square to move to? If not, don't play that move.
You're White. Deliver mate in one move without stalemating the king.
steps.hint: Your king on `f7` protects the square next to the black king.
steps.success: Mate! The queen is protected by the king. And note: if you had played `Qg6` it would have been stalemate and a draw.

mate-kr.title: Mate with king and rook
mate-kr.summary: The box method: shrink the king's prison rank by rank.

steps.text:
Mate with the rook is a bit harder, and its method is called **the box**: imagine the black king inside a box, and every rook move makes that box smaller.

Here the rook stands on the sixth rank, so the king is trapped in the last two ranks.

The rules:

1. The rook cuts off a rank or a file.
2. When the black king comes close to the rook, bring **your king** to meet him.
3. In the end the king is trapped on the last rank and the rook comes down with mate.
You're White. The king is trapped on the last rank. Deliver the mate.
steps.hint: The black king is already on the last rank. Finish it.
steps.success: Mate! Your king on `g6` was covering all the escape squares.

pawn-race.title: The pawn race
pawn-race.summary: King far away? Calculate the pawn's square before you run.

steps.text:
The square rule: draw an imaginary square from the pawn to the promotion square. Here the square runs from `a5` to `a8` to `d8` to `d5`.

**If the opponent's king can enter this square on his move, he will catch the pawn. If not, run and don't look back.**

The black king on `g6` is completely outside the square, so the pawn will promote on its own.
You're White. Promote the pawn. The black king will try to catch up, watch how he doesn't make it.
steps.hint: The black king is outside the square, which means your pawn is faster.
steps.success: You got a queen! Look: the black king kept running after you and didn't catch up. That's the difference between someone who calculates and someone who guesses.

lucena.title: The Lucena bridge
lucena.summary: The most famous winning idea in rook endgames: build a bridge.

steps.text:
Lucena: your pawn is on the seventh rank and close to promoting, but your king is out in front of it and the opponent will keep giving checks from far away.

The brilliant solution: **the bridge**. You put the rook on the fourth rank, preparing a place where your king can shelter from the checks.
Look at how the bridge is built: the rook on the fourth rank, the king walks to `c8` and `b8`, and the first check gets blocked by the rook with `Rb4`.

notes.0: First step: the rook comes to the fourth rank, getting ready for the bridge.
notes.2: The king steps out in front of the pawn toward c8.
notes.3: The opponent starts the checks from behind, and this is the most dangerous moment.
notes.6: The bridge is built! The rook blocks the check, and the pawn will promote on the next move.

philidor.title: The Philidor defense
philidor.summary: How to get a draw from a rook ending that looks lost.

steps.text:
Philidor: the opponent has a king and a pawn and a rook against your rook only. It looks lost, but there's a guaranteed draw:

**Your rook keeps giving checks from behind the king, so he can't advance, and the pawn alone isn't enough.**
Look at how the defense works: checks from behind until the king gives up, and then the pawn gets eaten.

notes.0: White pushed the pawn and is getting ready to promote.
notes.1: The first check from behind. The king has no place in front of him to hide.
notes.5: Check after check after check... the king can't find shelter.
notes.7: When the king moves away, the rook goes back behind the pawn: it will capture it next move, and the game is a draw.

queen-vs-pawn.title: Queen against a pawn about to promote
queen-vs-pawn.summary: Check, the king blocks his pawn, your king comes closer... and repeat.

steps.text:
The pawn is on the seventh rank and wants to promote, and you have only a queen and your king is far away. The famous method:

1. **Check with the queen** until the opponent's king stands **in front of his pawn**.
2. Then the pawn is blocked, so you can **bring your king closer** one move.
3. Repeat until your king arrives and you capture the pawn.

An important exception: if the pawn is on the **a or h file** (a rook pawn) or the **c or f file** (a bishop pawn), the opponent can get a draw with a stalemate idea, because the king gets trapped in the corner.

That's why in endgames, a central pawn is more dangerous than a wing pawn when it reaches the seventh.
You're White. Start the technique with the first check.
steps.hint: The queen on `a1` has a check on the sixth rank.
steps.success: The first check! The king will stand in front of his pawn, and then you bring your king one step closer... and repeat until you capture the pawn.

italian-deep.title: The Italian: school of attack
italian-deep.summary: e4 e5 and the bishop on c4 looks at Black's weakest square.

steps.text: The Italian is one of the oldest openings in history, and world champions still play it. The idea: the bishop goes to `c4` and looks at `f7`, the weakest square in Black's camp at the start, because it's protected only by the king.
The main line: White builds a strong pawn center with c3 and d4, and Black tries to pressure it.

notes.4: The bishop on c4: the key to the whole Italian.
notes.6: c3 prepares the central strike with d4.
notes.8: d4! White takes the center by force.
notes.11: A check with the bishop, and the game is still long, but White stands more comfortably.

steps.text: You're White in the Italian. Play the famous preparation move.
steps.hint: Prepare the central strike: move the pawn that will support d4.
steps.success: Right! c3 prepares d4, and if Black captures you recapture with the pawn and your center is stronger.

ruy-lopez.title: The Spanish (Ruy Lopez)
ruy-lopez.summary: The bishop on b5 pressures Black's knight and makes the game long and rich.

steps.text:
Ruy Lopez, a Spanish priest of the 16th century, had his name stuck to the deepest opening in chess. The bishop comes to `b5` and pressures the knight that protects the `e5` pawn.

Giants like Capablanca, Karpov and Carlsen built their fame on it.
The famous closed line: calm development, castling, and then a long fight over the center and the wings.

notes.5: a6: it asks the bishop "will you take or will you retreat?" - this is the start of the most famous line of the opening.
notes.6: The bishop keeps itself safe on the a2-g8 diagonal.
notes.12: c3 prepares d4 like in the Italian, but with more patience.

steps.text: You're Black against the Spanish. Play the move every player in the world asks.
steps.hint: Ask the bishop a question: will it take the knight or retreat?
steps.success: Exactly! a6 is the most famous move in the Spanish: it gains space and prepares b5 at the same time.

sicilian.title: The Sicilian: weapon of fighters
sicilian.summary: c5 instead of e5: Black refuses the draw from the first move.

steps.text:
1...c5! The Sicilian is the most famous reply to e4 at the professional level. Black attacks the center from the wing instead of from the center, and makes the game asymmetrical and full of fighting.

Fischer, Kasparov and Carlsen all fought with it.
The open Sicilian and the Najdorf version: Black castles on the kingside and strikes on the queenside.

notes.1: The idea: trade a wing pawn for a center pawn, and you'll have an extra center pawn in the endgame.
notes.4: White opened the center early - this is called the Open Sicilian.
notes.9: a6: this is the start of the "Najdorf", the most famous version in the whole Sicilian.

steps.text: You're Black and the opponent played e4. Declare war: play the first move of the Sicilian.
steps.hint: You won't answer e4 with the same. Attack the center from the wing.
steps.success: Welcome to the Sicilian! An asymmetrical game and a fight from the first move.

caro-kann.title: The Caro-Kann: Black's fortress
caro-kann.summary: c6 and then d5: a solid defense without locking in your bishop.

steps.text:
The Caro-Kann is the safest defense against e4: you prepare d5 with c6, so if White captures on d5 you recapture with the pawn and your pawn structure stays sound.

Its big advantage over the French: **your black bishop won't get locked behind your pawns**.
The classical line: Black develops his bishop to f5, then continues e6 and develops calmly.

notes.3: The main challenge: d5 in the face of White's center.
notes.6: The bishop comes out of the wall before e6 locks it in. This is the whole idea of the Caro-Kann.
notes.11: h6 opens a little window for the bishop on h7 if it's attacked.

steps.text: You're Black in the Caro-Kann. Play the challenge move.
steps.hint: c6 was the preparation for one move. Play it.
steps.success: Right! d5 is the direct challenge. If White captures, you recapture with the c6 pawn and your structure is sound.

french.title: The French: patience and stubbornness
french.summary: e6 and then d5: a solid pawn chain and a counterattack on its base.

steps.text:
The French is the defense of the patient: you build a pawn chain from `d5` to `e6`, and make your center solid like a wall.

Its only drawback: Black's dark-squared bishop gets locked behind the pawns. The good bishop and bad bishop lessons will teach you how to deal with it.
The Winawer version: Black hits the base of White's pawn chain on d4 with c5, and White has space and an attack on the kingside.

notes.4: Winawer: the bishop on b4 pins the knight and declares war.
notes.6: c5! The counterattack on the base of the pawn chain. This is the soul of the French.
notes.10: Black broke the pin on his knight and prepared his attack on the broken pawns.

steps.text: You're Black. Play the first move of the French.
steps.hint: This move prepares the d5 challenge from behind cover.
steps.success: Welcome to the French! e6 first, and then d5 challenges the center.

london.title: The London system: a way of life
london.summary: Almost the same setup against anything. Easy to learn, hard to break.

steps.text:
The London system is the most famous "lifestyle" opening: d4, Bf4, e3, Nf3, Nbd2 and c3, almost the same setup however Black plays.

Perfect if you want to play good chess without memorizing a library of lines. Even Carlsen plays it online.
The typical setup: a d4-e3-c3 pawn pyramid, a bishop on f4, knights on f3 and d2, and a king castled safely.

notes.2: The bishop comes out to f4 before e3 locks it in. This is the most important rule in the London.
notes.8: c3 supports the center and prepares e4 at the right time.
notes.12: Black challenged you with the bishop, and the bishop goes back to g3 and keeps looking along the diagonal.

steps.text: You're White playing the London. Play the star of the system.
steps.hint: The dark-squared bishop is the star of the London. Bring it out before you lock it in.
steps.success: Right! Bf4 before e3. If you had played e3 first the bishop would have been jailed.

queens-gambit.title: The Queen's Gambit: elegance of kings
queens-gambit.summary: c4: offering the wing pawn in return for control of the center.

steps.text:
The Queen's Gambit is one of the most refined openings: c4 offers the wing pawn, and if Black takes it, White takes the whole center with e4.

Hence the golden rule: **this gambit isn't really free** - White usually gets his pawn back.
The Queen's Gambit Declined: a long strategic battle over the d5 square and the c file.

notes.2: The gambit itself: pressure on d5 from the first minute.
notes.3: Black refused the pawn and fortified his center with e6 - this is the Queen's Gambit Declined.
notes.12: Black is preparing his bishop on b7 on the longest diagonal on the board.

steps.text: You're White. Declare the Queen's Gambit.
steps.hint: Black fortified d5. Pressure it with your wing pawn.
steps.success: Exactly! c4 is the gambit: if Black takes, e4 will give you the whole center.

kings-indian.title: The King's Indian: the scorpion defense
kings-indian.summary: Black gives up the center, castles, and then strikes one deadly blow.

steps.text:
The King's Indian is the defense of the daring: Black lets White take the whole center, develops his bishop on `g7` on the longest diagonal, castles... and then **blows up the center with e5**.

Fischer and Kasparov won legendary games with it.
The typical setup: a knight on f6, a fianchetto on g7, castling, and then e5 or c5 at the right time.

notes.2: Black isn't fighting for the center right now. Patience.
notes.5: The bishop on g7: a sniper on the long diagonal.
notes.10: e5! The blow everything before it was preparing.

steps.text: You're Black against d4. Start the King's Indian.
steps.hint: Start with the knight that looks at the center without occupying it.
steps.success: Right! Nf6 is the first step: it temporarily stops e4 and opens the road for the fianchetto and castling.

rook-mate-end.title: Rook mate on the edge
rook-mate-end.summary: Your king seals the escape, the rook delivers mate on the last rank.

steps.text:
Black's king is on the edge, and your king on `g6` covers its escape squares on the seventh rank: `f7`, `g7` and `h7`.

Only the last rank is left. The rook closes it with check.
Deliver mate with the rook.
steps.hint: The rook goes to the end of the rank, on the same line as Black's king.
steps.success: Mate! Your king covers the seventh rank and the rook closes the last one.

stalemate-trap.title: Watch out for stalemate
stalemate-trap.summary: One wrong move turns a win into a draw.

steps.text:
White is winning easily here, but if the queen goes to `g6` it **stalemates the king**: no check, and no square to move to, so the game is a draw.

The right move is the queen to `g7`, checkmate.
Win with checkmate, and do not stalemate the king.
steps.hint: The queen sits next to the king, protected by yours.
steps.success: Mate! And you avoided stalemate. Before any final move, ask: does the king have a square to go to?

queen-kiss-mate.title: The queen's kiss
queen-kiss-mate.summary: The queen next to the king, protected by yours, and mate is ready.

steps.text:
Black's king is in the corner on `a8`, and its escape squares are `a7`, `b7` and `b8`. Your king on `b6` covers `a7` and `b7`, and the queen on `c7` covers `b8`.

The queen lands next to the king on `a7` or `b7`, and Black cannot capture it because your king protects it.
Deliver mate.
steps.hint: Put the queen next to the king, on `a7` or `b7`.
steps.success: Mate! The queen is next to the king and yours protects it.

castle-early.title: Castle early
castle-early.summary: Castling puts the king in a safe place and brings the rook into play.

steps.text:
Castling is one move that does two things: **the king goes somewhere safer** and the rook leaves the corner and gets ready.

Conditions:

- Neither the king nor the rook has moved before.
- No pieces between them.
- The king is not in check.
- The king does not pass through or land on an attacked square.
The bishop and knight are out. Castle on the kingside.
steps.hint: Move the king two squares towards the rook.
steps.success: Now the king is safe and the rook is in the middle.

keep-developing.title: Keep developing
keep-developing.summary: After castling, bring out the remaining pieces and don't move at random.

steps.text:
White has castled, but the **knight and bishop** are still at home on `b1` and `c1`. These pieces must join the game before any attack.

Every opening move should do something useful: develop a piece or control the center.
Keep developing with a calm, useful move.
steps.hint: Bring out the knight that is still at home, or support the center with a pawn.
steps.success: Nice! `Nc3` develops a piece, and `d3` supports the center and opens the bishop.
